chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
title: Crashing into moonshiners in Henryetta
summary: Driving past a no-Negroes town, he rear-ends a car of moonshiners and the police take his side.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Anyway, we drove around for about a season, I guess, and one time, we were coming-- some of the boys would drive and I would drive

sometimes, in Henryetta, Oklahoma, a little town--I never did see this town--I mean, this sign--but they tell me at one time they had a sign up there, Nigger, read and run, if you can't read, run anyhow. I never did see that, but they told me some of them got together and they did move that sign, but no negroes or nothing were in this little town. But we would play other areas and we would come through there.

So one night we played somewhere and was coming through Henryetta and whoever the bus driver was, they let me have it to drive and they were resting up. Some drunk was in the middle of the street, in a car, and I was halfway asleep driving and I went right into the back of them and they had five gallons of whiskey and when I hit them, they didn't know what in the world had happen; they jumped out and ran. So the noise, the police came out and what in the world happened there? I said they were in the middle of the street, I couldn't see them,

what are they doing in the middle of the street there? And of course the officer, you're exactly right, and look here, they're moonshining too. We'll get them and don't you all worry, but I believe it messed up your radiator there, and then they just got to be as nice as they could. They said, we're going to get those guys, they're parked out here in the middle of the street and these guys ran into them and messed their car up. So they were looking after the guys because the whole thing was, they shouldn't have been parked where they were, but I ran into them because I was sleeping.

I'll never forget when the policeman first came up, Salva Sanders was still living then, and he said, go out and say something, don't wait until they say something to you, get out and tell them something, and so I got right out like I knew that they were in the wrong and of course they got right in my corner when they looked in there and saw all that corn whiskey. They said we've been after them anyway, we'll

get them. Then I think I called someone and got someone to put the bus in the garage; this town is only about forty eight miles from Tulsa, maybe fifty, and to show you how things are, (inaudible) black and white live there, but they don't give a darn about Henryetta, but that was the reputation that Henryetta had, that no blacks at all. But they were in our corner, nothing went on, we went back and got my bus fixed and came on in.

We made one little tour with that bus, a very good tour, and did so good and then the band loaned me money to buy this new school bus and I had it painted right then. So we were on time as far as that.
You went to New York in that in 1939?
Yeah, it wasn't too old then; that was the bus that I went in there on.
